}","refusal":null,"reasoning":"Let me work through this dossier.

Country (anonymised, looks Balkan — Montenegro, decriminalised 1977, Law on Prohibition of Discrimination 2010, Life Partnership 2020/2021, Pride 2013 with 2000 police). But I must not identify or substitute outside knowledge.

Facts:
- No criminalisation of same-sex conduct since 1977; no law criminalising trans identity or gender-nonconforming presentation. Explicitly: "A trans visitor faces no legal exposure for being trans or for presenting in a gender non-conforming way in public."
- Anti-discrimination law covers gender identity in employment, goods/services, education, health.
- Hate speech prohibition + penalty enhancements for LGBT-motivated offences; but applied unevenly, prosecutors downgrade to misdemeanour.
- No self-ID LGR; restrictive surgery/sterilisation requirement — resident-facing, not visitor exposure.
- Public hostility documented: hate speech, 222 online incidents 2023, psychologist in gender-nonconforming clothes attacked physically multiple times (police response monitored — i.e., present but monitored).
- Pride: first attempt 2011 cancelled after attacks; 2013 first Pride with 150 marchers and 2000 police, rock-throwing opponents, tear gas. Dated (2013, 2011).
- 51% of LGBT+ closeted (2018).
- 2012 travel guide: small gay scene, entrenched anti-gay opinion, discrimination/harassment when visible.

No documented trans-specific border friction, no facilities bans, no custody placement policy documented, no documented trans-visitor detention, no evidence of state threat-framing of trans people, no evidence of executions or imprisonment.

So worst documented features: societal hostility (tier 3) with... recourse? There is anti-discrimination law covering gender identity and hate-crime enhancements (paper, unevenly applied). Third-party violence including physical attacks on a visibly gender-nonconforming public figure (2023) — that's a documented pattern of some hostility, but the target was a local public figure, not a visitor. Pride violence is dated (2011, 2013).

Facilities/custody: not documented. Care services: anti-discrimination in health services documented; no documented trans-specific care denial for visitors. No documented bathroom bans, no strip-search-by-birth-sex practice documented.

Remedies: anti-discrimination law, hate-crime enhancements, though enforcement uneven; Pride protected by heavy police presence (state protection documented).

Now scoring. Compare to anchors.

0.35 tier: exclusion/registration/denial regimes with universal exposure — no such thing here. Nothing resembling Vellandra (entry register), Karthovia (police stops/unwritten instruction), Ostravia (hotel reporting).

0.55 tier: administrative registration requiring document matching, checkpoint holds, discretion-driven border secondary screening, health ward-by-document assignment, transit removal for "alarm". None documented here. No registration requirement, no checkpoint document-matching practice documented for trans people.

0.65 tier: mostly incidents where protection worked and remedy obtained; mixed. Hmm, 0.65 anchors describe jurisdictions with strong equality law, occasional enforcement failure, remedy working. This dossier: strong-ish formal protections (anti-discrimination with GI, hate crime enhancements though unevenly applied), documented societal hostility including physical attacks on visibly GNC person, dated Pride violence, no documented trans-specific visitor incidents, no documented remedy obtained by a trans visitor.

0.75 tier: jurisdictions where recourse works, moderate problems. Our dossier lacks documented evidence of remedy actually working for trans people (only the finding that hate-crime charges are downgraded — an unremedied exposure). Also public hostility is more documented than in 0.75 anchors.

0.85/0.95: clearly above this — those show functioning enforcement, trained border officers, etc. Not here.

So the case sits somewhere in the 0.55–0.70 band. Let me weigh.

Key: no criminalisation, no trans-specific legal restrictions applying to visitors, no documented state threat-framing, no facilities bans, no custody exposure documented. That pushes up. Against: documented societal hostility (hate speech, physical attacks on a visibly GNC person, 51% closeted, entrenched anti-gay opinion), uneven hate-crime enforcement, dated Pride violence requiring 2000 police for 150 marchers.

Rule 19: social hostility is real weight. The 2023 physical attacks on the psychologist: several physical attacks, police response monitored (implies police engagement, maybe monitoring). That's a documented pattern of hostility in the recent past, but targeted at a local public figure.

Rule 7: individual incidents — pattern? "hate comments, threats and several physical attacks" — several attacks against one person, part of a documented hate-speech trend (222 incidents). That's a pattern of societal hostility, though not trans-visitor-specific.

Also rule 20: activist visibility isn't danger; local sphere (closeted 51%, family rejection) — visitor doesn't enter that sphere.

Rule 2: sexuality law is secondary; here there's no criminalisation at all.

Practical exposure for a visitor: hotel check-in with documents mismatching presentation — no documentation of refusal. Bathroom access — no documentation of restriction. Police stops — no documentation of harassment of trans people; Pride protection shows police can act protectively, though 2013.

I'd say this is a generally safe destination with a moderately conservative society and reasonably protective but unevenly enforced law. Analogous to the 0.65 tier but with less demonstrated remedy-working and more documented hostility. Something around 0.62–0.66. I'll say 0.63.

Hmm, consider whether the anchors 0.65 cases all feature a specific incident plus functioning remedy. Our dossier has no remedy demonstrated for trans people (only formal law + an adverse finding about prosecutors). And the 0.75 anchors have working remedies. So below 0.65 maybe. But 0.55 anchors feature universal registration/checkpoint exposures we lack.

I'll settle at 0.62. Or 0.60. Let me think about the "band implication" note in rule 21: "no criminalisation plus functioning institutions does not anchor a jurisdiction at Reduced Risk" — but that applies to dossiers documenting universal-exposure practices or discrimination prevalence at scale. Do we have discrimination prevalence at scale? The 28.1% corporate-policy figure is about employers mentioning sexual orientation — not a trans-specific discrimination prevalence survey. The 51% closeted is LGBT-wide, 2018, and about being closeted, not discrimination prevalence in a setting a traveller enters. So rule 17 limits it. No trans-specific prevalence survey.

So no universal-exposure measure documented; no state threat-framing documented. There is documented societal hostility with partial recourse (law exists, enforcement uneven). Per precedence ladder, worst feature is tier 3 (documented societal hostility with thin-ish recourse) — actually recourse exists on paper and hate-crime enhancements exist. So tier 3 or between 3 and 5.

Compare: 0.65 anchors have remedy demonstrated; ours doesn't but also lacks a traveller-facing adverse incident. So maybe 0.62–0.65. I'll go 0.63.
